cl_can_strain_labels.q: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed?
cl_can_strain_labels.short: Mostly not. In 41,201 lab-tested US weed samples, indica, hybrid and sativa labels barely matched the mix of terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell. Strain names did a bit better.
cl_can_strain_labels.but: The labels came from a strain website, not the bags. And nobody measured how the weed felt.
how: Researchers used lab results for about 90,000 flower samples that licensed growers sent for testing in six US states, 2013 to 2021. Labels came from a strain website, matched by name.
In 41,201 samples high in THC, the three labels were all mixed up in their terpenes. Sativa was twice as common in one smell type, rich in terpinolene, but most of those were still hybrid.
Strain names did better: for 26 of 41 widely grown names, different growers' products were more alike than chance. For 13 they weren't, and two, LSD and Durban Poison, were less alike.
A small Dutch study tested two coffee-shop strains, one sativa-type and one indica-type. They had similar THC but different terpenes, and each varied a lot from bag to bag.
cl_can_strain_labels.rate: One very large set of lab records, but it checked only smell compounds, used a strain website's labels instead of the packages, and measured no effects on people.

cl_gen_family_craft.q: How can I get a family member who refuses help into treatment?
cl_gen_family_craft.short: Family skills training called CRAFT worked best in trials. In one, 64 in 100 relatives who'd refused help started treatment within 6 months, against 30 and 13 with other approaches.
cl_gen_family_craft.but: Just four small US trials, and three came from the teams that created CRAFT.
how: The biggest trial had 130 family members, mostly women, living with someone with a drinking problem. Each got one of three approaches by chance, about 12 hours each.

Within 6 months, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment after CRAFT. It was 30 after training for a family confrontation, and 13 after counselling to join Al-Anon. Seven in 10 families chose not to hold the confrontation.
Pooling four trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, relatives started treatment about 3 times as often with CRAFT as with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches: 67 against 18 in 100.
Family members felt less depressed and angry after 6 months in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment. With no group left without help, no approach can take the credit.
cl_gen_family_craft.rate: Families were assigned by chance, and the gap was big and pointed the same way in every trial. But there are only four small US trials, mostly from CRAFT's creators.

cl_benzo_stopping_suddenly.q: Is it dangerous to stop benzos suddenly?
cl_benzo_stopping_suddenly.short: It can be, but two expert reviews don't say how often. Both warn of seizures; the only count is 2 of 11 prisoners on very high doses, in 1961.
cl_benzo_stopping_suddenly.but: These are expert reviews, not studies. Their seizure warnings give no rates, and one cites no source at all.
how: One review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use, in about 15 to 30 in 100 people. That figure comes from the author's own earlier review.

Symptoms listed include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound. They can feel like the problem the pills were for, and sleeping pills can bring back worse sleep even after a few nights.
Both reviews warn of seizures after stopping suddenly; one says severe reactions can happen even with slow tapering. But it calls most reports anecdotes, and the other cites no source.
The only count: in 1961, 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months were switched to a dummy pill. Ten had withdrawal, and 2 had seizures.
cl_benzo_stopping_suddenly.rate: Two expert reviews, not new studies. Their figures are second-hand, the seizure warnings give no rates, and the only count comes from 11 prisoners on very high doses in 1961.

cl_gen_festival_policing.q: Do police and sniffer dogs at festivals stop people taking drugs?
cl_gen_festival_policing.short: Not by much, going by what people said. With sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 said they'd still use drugs, against 77 with no police, in an Australian online survey.
cl_gen_festival_policing.but: It's what people said they'd do at a made-up festival, not what they really did.
how: 2,115 Australian festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, took an online survey. Each read about a made-up festival with no police, and one with police, riot police, sniffer dogs or police working with health workers.
With any police, 70 in 100 said they'd use drugs and 53 in 100 that they'd carry drugs in, against 77 and 63 with no police. With sniffer dogs, 47 in 100 said they'd carry drugs in.
Slightly more said they'd buy drugs inside the festival when police were there: 40 against 37 in 100. The authors worry those drugs may not be what they're sold as, which wasn't checked.
Police working with health services made almost no difference: 75 in 100 still said they'd use drugs. The survey didn't ask how much people would take.
cl_gen_festival_policing.rate: One online survey of people who chose to take part, about made-up scenarios. What people say they'd do isn't always what they do, and some of the paper's statistics don't add up.

general.statement: Confronting someone as a family works best to get them into treatment.
general.why: In one trial, 30 in 100 relatives started treatment after confrontation training, against 64 in 100 after CRAFT skills training. Seven in 10 families never held the confrontation.

general.statement: Family members only feel better if their loved one starts treatment.
general.why: In one trial, family members felt less depressed and angry in every group, whether or not the relative started treatment. With no group left without help, no approach can take the credit.

general.statement: In a survey, most festival-goers said sniffer dogs would stop them using drugs.
general.why: With dogs, 66 in 100 still said they'd use drugs, against 77 with no police. These were answers to made-up scenarios, not real behaviour.

benzodiazepines.statement: Benzo withdrawal can feel like the anxiety or sleep problems the pills were for.
benzodiazepines.why: Both reviews say withdrawal symptoms can resemble the original problem. They are expert reviews, so this is second-hand.

benzodiazepines.statement: Reviews that warn of seizures after stopping benzos say how often they happen.
benzodiazepines.why: Both reviews read warn of seizures, but neither gives a rate. The only count is 2 of 11 prisoners in 1961, in conditions unlike usual use.
